title: AI infrastructure builders have much less internal financing headroom than chip suppliers
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
summary: Six large US data-centre builders invested almost their entire adjusted operating cash flow during the recent AI build-out. Three semiconductor suppliers increased investment too, but generated enough cash to invest, repay debt and increase distributions. Julian Kozlowski, Juan M. Sánchez and Nicholas Sullivan locate the financing pressure in the builders. It is easy to miss in sector-level leverage ratios. Across ten large technology companies, debt grew in dollars while declining relative to an even faster-growing asset base.

The article first compares asset-weighted balance sheets for ten firms with those of the other publicly traded US firms in the sample. Between 2023 and early 2026, hyperscaler debt fell from nearly 30% to roughly 25% of assets. The group remained less levered than the comparison firms. Net shareholder distributions, comprising dividends and repurchases after equity issuance, fell from about 4% of assets in 2022 to approximately 2% in early 2026, close to the ratio for the other firms. Operating income relative to assets, measured before depreciation and amortisation in the chart, rose from around 21% in 2023 to 25% in early 2026, against roughly 13% for the comparison group. Profitability gives these firms substantial capacity to fund investment internally. These three charts cannot show which firms need to borrow at the margin.

The authors therefore reconstruct sources and uses of cash. They include R&D in investment and add it back to reported operating cash flow because the expense was originally deducted there. Investment is net investing cash outflow plus R&D. The funds available to meet it are adjusted operating cash flow plus net debt issuance, less net shareholder payouts and cash accumulation. A drawdown of cash releases funding. A buildup of cash absorbs it. The simplified identity omits a small residual for other financing flows and exchange-rate effects (financing section, note 2). Neither adjusted operating cash flow nor the earlier profitability ratio is conventional free cash flow. The two have different definitions and answer different questions.

The financing table compares average quarterly flows during 2012 Q1–2018 Q4 and 2024 Q4–2026 Q2, in billions of GDP-deflated dollars. The six builders are Alphabet, Amazon, IBM, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle. Their investment rose from $34.59 billion to $196.38 billion per quarter, an increase of 467.8%. Adjusted operating cash flow grew from $44.46 billion to $197.52 billion. Subtracting investment leaves $1.14 billion per quarter in the recent period, before distributions or changes in cash. The same arithmetic yielded $9.87 billion in the earlier period, despite the much smaller scale of the business. These are period averages across the group, so an individual company's peak funding requirement could differ substantially.

Net debt issuance filled part of the gap between the builders' investment and their other uses of funds. It rose from $3.23 billion to $30.17 billion per quarter. Two details qualify the idea that the builders financed the surge simply by cancelling buybacks or running down cash. Quarterly net shareholder payouts actually rose from $12.04 billion to $26.84 billion. They fell relative to adjusted operating cash flow, from 27.1% to 13.6%. Cash accumulation likewise rose in dollars, from $1.21 billion to $4.43 billion, while declining from 2.7% to 2.2% of adjusted operating cash flow. The builders could borrow more on net even as aggregate hyperscaler leverage fell. Gross issuance and its refinancing component cannot be recovered from this table.

For Broadcom, Intel and Nvidia together, the recent quarterly averages were $40.98 billion of adjusted operating cash flow and $22.68 billion of investment, leaving $18.30 billion before financing and distributions. Their adjusted cash generation grew 288.3% between the two periods, compared with 165.4% growth in investment. Net debt issuance of $1.10 billion became net repayment of $0.79 billion per quarter. Net payouts rose from 28.1% to 34.4% of adjusted operating cash flow, while cash accumulation rose from 0.5% to 5.7%. Apple is included in the ten-firm charts but excluded from both table panels because its chip and cloud activities primarily serve its own consumer products. The two subgroups therefore do not sum to the full chart sample.

The authors infer that the builders are increasingly dependent on sustained profits, retained earnings and access to financing. For a credit investor, the distinction is between a group that can cover investment on average and one that can cover investment and its other commitments if earnings weaken. The article explicitly omits future lease and purchase obligations and remaining performance obligations from the analysis. Those contracts may affect both financing needs and future revenues, and the table gives no maturity schedule. It also provides no bond spreads, funding costs or evidence that this risk is mispriced. The study identifies where to examine refinancing and commitment risk without establishing that a borrower faces distress.

questions.question: How large is each builder's funding requirement once contractual payments fall due?
questions.detail: The six builders retained only $1.14 billion per quarter on average after measured investment. That estimate aggregates firms and excludes forward commitments. Start with the authors' cited Review article, then match construction payments, leases, purchase obligations and debt maturities to issuer cash-flow statements and available liquidity. The timing would determine which issuer could sustain its programme through a period of tighter financing.

questions.question: How much spending could management actually defer if operating cash flow fell?
questions.detail: The financing table shows that shareholder payouts still rose in dollars. It does not identify the flexibility of repurchases, dividends or partly completed projects. Company authorisations, contractual cancellation terms and capital-project schedules could distinguish discretionary distributions from unavoidable outlays. That distinction matters for the size and timing of external financing under stress.

questions.question: How independent is the suppliers' cash surplus from builders' willingness to invest?
questions.detail: The suppliers retained financing headroom while the builders absorbed most of theirs. The table cannot establish whether those outcomes depend on the same orders. Contemporary segment revenue, customer-concentration and order-commitment disclosures could link supplier cash receipts to builder spending. Evidence that the same buyers drive both sides would change the expected diversification benefit of holding their securities together.
